paragraphs: Swamiji held that spirituality is India's backbone, and that we need a guide to show us that path. A Hindu, in his view, was one who accepted that his religion is pure spirituality.

He recalled a conversation in a village in Kashmir. Chatting with an elderly Muslim woman, he gently asked her what her religion was. Her face lit up, and in her own tongue she praised the Lord and said that, by God's grace, she was a Muslim. Her answer overflowed with gratitude and conviction.
Then he asked a Hindu the same question. The man simply replied, flatly, that he was a Hindu. Nothing more.

The contrast stayed with Swamiji. It reminded him of a great word from the Katha Upanishad: shraddha, a wonderful, living faith, the kind young Nachiketa showed. Spreading this genuine faith, he said, was the mission of his life. Such faith is one of the most powerful forces in humanity and in every religion.
And it begins with faith in yourself. One person may be a tiny bubble and another a towering wave, but behind both lies the same infinite ocean.
learn: Whatever you believe in, hold it with warmth and conviction, not as a label you shrug off. And start with faith in yourself: you may feel small next to others, but the same limitless potential stands behind everyone.
